description: We are LarpCorp, a multidisciplinary team of coders, designers, and science enthusiasts working on the challenge. Excited to collaborate, learn, and solve real-world problems this weekend!
summary:
Ask a climate dashboard what is happening to Ghana and you get one number for the whole country. Split it north from south and the answer changes: the south is warming at a rate that holds up, the north is not.

TerraTrend is an interactive Earth-change observatory that helps people investigate where the environment is changing, how quickly, and how strong the evidence is. Users select a country, administrative region, or custom boundary on a 3D globe, choose a measurement and time period, and explore NASA and NOAA records of temperature, rainfall, soil moisture, wind, and vegetation.

The platform calculates rates of change, confidence intervals, and statistical significance, compares two regions, and screens for relationships between Earth-system variables. Results include source information and explanations at plain, student, or researcher reading levels.

Built for "Be An Earth System Trend Detective!", TerraTrend connects open Earth-observation data with accessible investigation tools. It helps students, educators, researchers, and communities explore local environmental change while keeping uncertainty and data limitations visible.
details:
What it does

TerraTrend is a globe you can question. Spin to a country, pick a region, or draw the exact patch of land you care about with a lasso. Choose one of twenty environmental variables, from air temperature to root-zone soil moisture to vegetation greenness. A few seconds later you get a chart, a rate of change per decade, a confidence interval, and a straight answer on whether the change is statistically significant.

Before the answer arrives, the app tells you where the numbers will come from, how many source cells or stations fall inside your shape, and roughly how heavy the request is. If a place cannot support a verdict, it says so instead of drawing a line through three points.

How it works

The backend is Python. It pulls monthly observations directly from NASA services: MERRA-2 through GES-DISC OPeNDAP, Giovanni, AppEEARS for MODIS vegetation, and GLDAS through the Hydrology Time Series tool, plus NOAA station records. Every grid cell is clipped to the real polygon and weighted by cos(latitude), because a degree of longitude is not a degree of latitude.

Then the statistics. Trends come from Theil-Sen, which takes the median of all pairwise slopes so one volcanic year cannot drag the line. Significance comes from a tie-corrected Mann-Kendall test with an AR(1) correction computed on detrended residuals and floored at 1, so negative autocorrelation cannot manufacture certainty. An OLS regression runs alongside as a cross-check, and the two methods are reported as agreeing or disagreeing instead of being quietly merged into one number.

The frontend is vanilla JavaScript and Three.js. The Earth, the day/night terminator, the projected boundaries and the teleconnection arcs are all generated in the browser. Live satellite layers come from NASA GIBS at whatever date you choose.

Two things beyond a single trend

Compare mode takes two areas and builds a paired difference series, A minus B, over matching years, which is the correct test when both regions share the same weather. Interconnections mode splits two series into trend, seasonal climatology and residual anomaly, searches lags in both directions, then runs partial correlation and Granger tests and applies Benjamini-Hochberg control across the whole family of tests. That last step is what stops a few hundred pairings from producing a handful of fake discoveries.

The assistant

Ask a question in plain English and it answers at your reading level: plain, student or researcher. The language model never writes the numbers. It selects from a bank of pre-audited statements keyed to a hash of the computed evidence, so it can be vague but it cannot invent a slope or a p-value. Every explanation is logged with the evidence hash it was built from.

Why we trust it

We checked the engine against NASA's own outputs rather than against itself: 240 months of real MERRA-2 granules for Ghana and Europe, 108 of 108 AppEEARS NDVI monthly means matching exactly, 324 of 324 GLDAS values matching at their declared rounding. Hundreds of automated tests cover the statistics, the service parsers and the frontend contracts.

Being an Earth system trend detective means being willing to say "not significant". Both halves of Ghana have plenty of data. The south shows significant warming and significant wetting. The north shows a small warming slope that does not clear the test. Both of those are results. Reporting only the first one would be the easiest thing in the world and the least useful.

What we used

Python 3 with NumPy, SciPy, netCDF4 and Requests; vanilla JavaScript, Three.js and WebGL shaders for the globe; SQLite on disk for the cache; Docker and a one-command start script so it runs anywhere. NASA data and imagery, NOAA station records and Natural Earth boundaries are all listed in the fields below.

Code

Everything is open source: https://github.com/LarpCorporation/Terratrend

Clone it, run ./start.sh 8517, and the whole thing is up on your own machine. Deployment config for Render and Vercel is included.
